newsitem.title: BRAZIL: TENNIS-BRAZIL FIGHT BACK AGAINST UNITED STATES.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-BRAZIL FIGHT BACK AGAINST UNITED STATES.

text.p: Brazil fought their way back into their Davis Cup match against the United States on Saturday, winning the doubles to ensure a tense final day for their opponents.

Unrated Jaime Oncins and Gustavo Kuerten, backed by a typically rowdy South American crowd, reduced the U.S. lead to 2-1 with a remarkable straight sets victory over Alex O'Brien and Richey Reneberg, two of the world's top doubles players.
The Brazilians, rank outsiders to win the tie, won 6-2 6-4 7-5 in a match which featured several disputed line calls and left the U.S. pair wondering what went wrong.

"My brain was on that drum up in the stands, my forehand was in the field outside the court, my serve was back in Texas and my backhand was in Sao Paulo," said O'Brien, thoroughly disillusioned with his own performance.
Reneberg, who has the 1995 Australian Open doubles among his titles, was equally critical of himself after losing his first four service games.
"My serve wasn't good, I didn't get to the net enough and when I did, I missed a lot of volleys," he said. "It was just one of those days that you have to write off."
Brazil cruised through the first set and took the second after a controversial last game on Kuerten's serve.
The U.S. appeared as though they had won the game when a Kuerten second serve appeared to go out but it was called in, causing a wave of protest from the American camp.
Captain Tom Gullikson said: "The umpire's job is to enforce the rules and today I don't think he did that properly."

The third set went with serve until the 11th game, when Reneberg was broken for the fifth time after making unforced errors on crucial successive points. Oncins held serve in the next game to spark off huge celebrations in the stands.
The 5,000 fans greeted the U.S. pair with a deafening chorus of jeers and played samba drums and blew horns between points, leading to two threats from the referee to penalise the home team a point.
Reneberg and O'Brien, however, said they were not distracted and blamed their own poor performances.

Oncins, ranked 156th in the world and the hero when Brazil reached the semi-finals in 1992, said: "They may have more grand slam titles but it was our pair who had the determination and the will to win."
